d779b61f11dcc58c7773de4821732ec4.text: Operation Red Nose Williams Lake is gearing up to provide safe rides home this holiday season. Volunteers will be at the ready this holiday season in Williams Lake to provide safe rides home. Operation Red Nose (ORN) is returning and will be available from 9 p.m. to 3 a.m. on Nov. 27, 28 and Dec. 4, 5, 11, 12, 18, 19 and 31. The service aimed at preventing impaired driving does not compete with taxi services, and instead provides people rides home within a 30-minute driving radius of Williams Lake in their own vehicles accompanied by a driver in a vehicle provided by local car dealerships. Rides are by donation, with all proceeds supporting local youth sports, including the the Williams Lake Minor Hockey Rep U18 Female and U18 Integrated teams, Cariboo Chilcotin Youth Fiddle Society, Cariboo Gymnastics Association and Cariboo Cheer All-Stars. The year’s program is being run by a team of Williams Lake Community Policing volunteers chaired by Donna Bergen, who has volunteered several years during ORN. “It’s coming along really good, so I feel pretty good,” Bergen said, adding she enjoys helping the community. “When you have people that you know that have died because of a drunk driver, you want to help people who are intoxicated get home.” According to a news release, outgoing ORN coordinator Deborah Pickering will continue to share her knowledge, as well as Dave Dickson, who was the first person to bring ORN to Williams Lake. ORN will once again be headquartered out of Heartland Toyota. “Year after year, support from the dealerships and party-goers who call for a ride ensure the program’s success, for which we are grateful,” the release stated. Bergen encourages anyone interested in volunteering with ORN to email her at donnabergen2022@gmail.com or call 250-267-9901. They’ll have to get a criminal record check. Each of the local youth sports receiving donation proceeds will also be supplying drivers.

aa416ee1136edc0ee1c53feb949fffc7.text: Environment Canada is warning of moderate to strong gusty winds across the Okanagan and much of B.C.’s Southern Interior later this afternoon (Saturday, Nov. 7) and continuing through Sunday evening. ​A special weather statement covers the Okanagan Connector, Coquihalla Highway, South Thompson, Nicola and other Interior regions. ​Southeasterly winds are expected to strengthen later Saturday, with gusts of 60 to 80 km/h across the Interior. Winds are forecast to peak by Sunday morning before easing. ​An incoming cold front is expected to push southwesterly winds into the region early Sunday afternoon, with gusts potentially reaching up to 90 km/h in western areas before calming down by Sunday night. ​Officials say local utility outages are possible and drivers should be prepared for crosswinds. Residents are advised to secure loose objects outdoors. ​The statement comes after a powerful coastal storm Friday that brought heavy rain and high winds to Vancouver Island. A separate rain warning remains in effect for the Fraser Canyon, where up to 50 mm of rain is expected through Sunday morning.

Norah Caldwell, co-author of the "Where is Lisa Marie Young?" book, was asked to help write the book by sister and Island Crime Podcast host Laura Palmer. The book "Where is Lisa Marie Young: The Disappearance of an Indigenous Woman and Her Family's Fight to Bring Her Home" has been released. Family and friends of an Indigenous woman who went missing in Nanaimo nearly 25 years ago, hope a new book sparks interest and possibly new leads in the investigation. _Where_ is _Lisa Marie Young: The Disappearance of an Indigenous Woman and Her Family’s Fight to Bring Her Home_ has been released by TouchWood Editions, delving into details about the woman whose last known whereabouts were in Nanaimo on June 30, 2002. It is co-authored by Carolann Bosma and Norah Caldwell and inspired by the Laura Palmer Island Crime Podcast. Speaking at a book reading at Nanaimo North Library Wednesday, Nov. 4, Bosma, Young’s foster sister, said penning the book was “definitely a journey emotionally, with lots of highs, lots of lows.” It was also an emotional process because there is still a lot of grief. Nanaimo RCMP have maintained constant communication, Bosma told the News Bulletin, and both hope the book is the catalyst for new leads. “That was one of the reasons why I agreed to write the book, is because we’re always looking for different ways to reach out to the community and our ultimate goal is to have Lisa come home,” said Bosma. “I’m really hoping the book is able to get into the hands of someone who possibly might have information and it’s almost like a quiet conversation with that person. Testing is underway to determine if a captured grizzly bear in Bella Coola is linked to the recent attack that claimed the life of a mother and daughter. In a Friday, Nov. 6 Facebook post, BC Conservation Officer Service (BCCOS) stated one grizzly bear has been captured. “In coordination with wildlife biologists and the provincial wildlife veterinarian from the Ministry of Water, Land and Resource Stewardship, the bear will be safely cared for while assessments are completed,” the post reads. Family has identified the victims as Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20 who failed to return after going for a walk on the Snooka West Trail. They were killed in a suspected grizzly bear attack less than a year after several school children and one adult were left with serious injuries. A range of tools, including forensic DNA matching, distinctive physical measurements and other animal-specific characteristics, will be used by BCCOS to help determine if the captured bear is involved in the attacks. A team of Conservation Officers remain on the ground as trapping efforts continue. “Any bear confirmed to be responsible will be dispatched to protect public safety; unrelated bears will be released,” the Facebook post further stated. “Conservation Officers also have forensic and other evidence from the 2025 Bella Coola attack, which will be compared with evidence from any captured bears undergoing assessment.” The public is urged to continue avoiding the West Snooka Trail area where several bear sightings near the area of the fatal attacks have been reported. “This is a devastating and deeply unfortunate event that has had a profound impact on the families, the Nuxalk Nation, and the broader Bella Coola community. 91bd4284e42db74024ac97610a19d4a4.text: Haan Palcu-Chang, Top Chef Canada Season 11 finalist and the chef behind Favorites Thai BBQ's Toronto Life Best New Restaurant win, has a debut cookbook, Recipes from a Transylvanian Village. Born to a Romanian mother and Taiwanese father, Haan Palcu-Chang grew up straddling two culinary worlds. After building his name in kitchens across Paris, Copenhagen, Singapore, Toronto, and Vancouver, he stepped away from the restaurant industry and relocated with his family to Salt Spring Island. He was a Top Chef Canada Season 11 finalist and the chef behind Favorites Thai BBQ’s Toronto Life Best New Restaurant win. Alongside the accolades and moves, he cooked up an online following of more than 250,000 people who tune in for his food content. Now his debut cookbook, Recipes from a Transylvanian Village, shares his story about two homelands on one plate. The story of heritage, reinvention, and a chef who refuses to be boxed into one tradition marks Palcu-Chang’s first full-length published work. “Romanian cuisine is a really, really underappreciated and underrepresented cuisine, in restaurants and cookbooks, but it’s a cuisine really deep in tradition and vast in diversity,” he said. “We want to get people thinking about it and then trying it.” Getting there meant a series of meals crafted for his Romanian grandmother to taste, savour and ideally reminisce on. The goal was to inspire nostalgia, hitting the exact flavour profile of her childhood. “Romanian food was part of my life, but these recipes were not necessarily part of my grandmother’s repertoire,” he said of piecing them together from matriarchal memories while leaning on his skills as a chef. “Recipe books aren’t usually very informative, they’re filled with very sporadic measurements and things that aren’t super helpful.” It meant getting grandma to taste the things a million times “until I hit the memory receptors.” Sometimes he knocked it out of the park, others took some retakes. 1194b3b03b08707cd3b950d2592e417e.text: Owning a home is billed as a way to build wealth, but amid climate-related disasters, for many it's beginning to feel like a trap. To Sierra Isley, the American Dream brings to mind a home ringed by a white picket fence. “The house in the suburbs is just what you’re taught growing up,” the 26-year-old said. “You know, that’s what you see on TV.” What she wanted for her life was a bit different from that picket-fence ideal, but she still saw the prospect of buying her first house two years ago as a chance to live out what she called “that big dream that everybody has as a kid.” Isley and her girlfriend, Jamie, were moving from Philadelphia to Asheville, North Carolina, and found a home they liked, a three-bedroom brick house with lots of natural light and a big tree out front. With some help from their parents, they put down a deposit and got their offer accepted. But when they went to sign the closing papers, a complication got in the way: The house had a huge lien on it. After consulting with lawyers, they decided to break the contract and hunt for an apartment to rent in Asheville. It was a blessing in disguise. One month later, while Sierra and Jamie were still unpacking boxes and building furniture, the remnants of Hurricane Helene turned Asheville into a disaster zone. The basement of their apartment flooded, but they were luckier than some of their neighbors, whose homes had been destroyed. Owning a home has long been seen as a cornerstone of the American Dream—a way to build wealth that you could use one day to pay for your children’s education and fund your retirement. That arrangement was always more precarious than it was made out to be. But as fires and floods damage homes and drive up insurance rates, pouring your life savings into a house has become riskier than ever. a9a38bd54821939f9fa9f27ed388cbb0.text: The United Nations climate conference COP31 is set to open on Monday in Antalya, Turkiye, against the backdrop of the US-led war on Iran, which has underscored the world’s attachment to fossil fuels. Turkiye has said it would centre electrification on the COP31 agenda, launching the non-binding 35-by-35 Global Electrification Pledge, which aims to make electricity account for at least 35 percent of global energy demand by 2035. Electricity currently accounts for about one-fifth of global total final energy consumption, according to the International Energy Agency. Turkiye says the “35 by 35” will speed up the shift to renewable sources of energy while strengthening energy security. “This year’s energy crisis has shocked us… everyone now understands that energy that you import is energy that you do not control,” the COP31 president and Turkiye’s environment minister, Murat Kurum, said on Thursday. “Electrification is the answer. It protects communities from volatile global markets and cuts emissions.” COP31’s aim is “to usher in the age of electricity”, he said. However, climate advocates have criticised the pledge, arguing it does not require that additional electricity come from low-carbon sources. This has set up a debate on whether electrification alone should count as climate progress. notification-importantGet instant alerts and updates based on your interests. 2c713fc7cb8099e3847b5e0a7037fc6b.text: Courtesy of Jillian PretzelThe author's mother, 62, doesn't wear any makeup. My mom is 62 and she's never gotten Botox or filler. She doesn't even wear makeup. These days, that's rare, especially where we live. My mom and I were both born and raised in Southern California, and here, beauty standards are high. Plastic surgery and other enhancements are common. Microneedling, chemical peels, microdermabrasion, and LED light treatment services are a "must" for many. But my mom has shown me that's not the only way to approach aging. Her decision to skip cosmetic products and procedures taught me something important about aging — something I didn't fully understand until recently. A couple of weeks ago, after a particularly long session staring at my crows' feet in the mirror, I asked my mom why she never wears makeup. When I was growing up, she'd wear it sparingly: some eyeliner and a touch of lip gloss for a special occasion. However, for the last couple of decades, the only thing she's worn on her face is lotion. Standing at my kitchen counter, I asked if there was a certain day she decided: "Makeup isn't for me." As it turns out, there was. My mom told me it started during her freshman year of college. She'd seen her roommate put on makeup — and was horrified. The author is grateful that she grew up with her mom's example. According to her, the roommate spent nearly an hour every morning applying expensive products. Then, after brushing on a few thick layers of mascara, she'd open a safety pin and use the point to separate each individual eyelash. "I already couldn't believe the time and money she spent on her face," Mom said. "But I was shocked that she was willing to put a pin next to her eye. What if there was an earthquake?
